Lecture 26

Laplace transforms and operational identities

We define the Laplace transform with its half-plane of absolute convergence and prove that it is analytic there. We fix the 0−0^-0− convention for initial impulses, prove the operational rules, and apply them to delayed pulses, a periodic input and the transfer function of the oscillator.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Find the half-plane of absolute convergence of a transform, and distinguish it from an exponential-order bound and from the domain of its formula.
  • Compute transforms with the operational rules and state the half-plane of each.
  • Transform an equation with an initial impulse from the data at 0−0^-0−, without double counting.
  • Relate the transfer function H(s)H(s)H(s) of the oscillator to its impulse response, its steady response H(σ)eσtH(\sigma)\ee^{\sigma t}H(σ)eσt and its frequency response H(iω)H(\iu\omega)H(iω).

The Fourier integral of Lectures 23 and 25 needs a signal integrable over the whole time axis. A growing exponential such as et\ee^tet is not tempered (Lecture 22), so Lecture 24 gives it no transform either. We now multiply a signal of an initial-value problem, given for t>0t>0t>0, by e−st\ee^{-st}e−st with a complex sss and integrate from 000 to ∞\infty∞. For large Re⁡s\Re sRes this defines an analytic function on a half-plane, the Laplace transform.

26.1 The transform and its half-plane

A function fff on (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞) is piecewise continuous in the sense of Lecture 22’s standing rules if on every bounded subinterval it is continuous except at finitely many points, with finite one-sided limits there. Near t=0t=0t=0 it may be unbounded, as t−1/2t^{-1/2}t−1/2 is.

Definition 26.1 (Laplace transform). Let fff be piecewise continuous on (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞). For a real number ccc we say that fff is transformable at ccc if ∫0∞e−ct∣f(t)∣ ⁣dt<∞,\int_0^\infty\ee^{-ct}\abs{f(t)}\dd t<\infty ,∫0∞​e−ct∣f(t)∣dt<∞,(26.1) an improper integral at 000 and at ∞\infty∞ (GM 27). The function fff is transformable if it is transformable at some real ccc, and then its abscissa of absolute convergence cfc_fcf​ is the infimum of the numbers ccc at which fff is transformable, a real number or −∞-\infty−∞. The Laplace transform of fff is F(s)=L ⁣[f](s)=∫0∞e−stf(t) ⁣dtF(s)=\LT{f}(s)=\int_0^\infty\ee^{-st}f(t)\dd tF(s)=L[f](s)=∫0∞​e−stf(t)dt(26.2) for every complex sss such that fff is transformable at Re⁡s\Re sRes.

Because 000 is not a point of (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞), piecewise continuity on (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞) requires nothing at t=0t=0t=0; this is why t−1/2t^{-1/2}t−1/2 is allowed, unlike in Lecture 23’s class. Where we need the value f(0+)f(0^+)f(0+) or a bound near 000, we ask instead that fff be piecewise continuous on every bounded interval [0,β][0,\beta][0,β] in the sense of Lecture 23, which makes fff bounded near 000. We write the transform of a function with the corresponding capital letter, F=L ⁣[f]F=\LT fF=L[f], G=L ⁣[g]G=\LT gG=L[g], Y=L ⁣[y]Y=\LT yY=L[y]. For t>0t>0t>0 we have ∣e−st∣=e−tRe⁡s\abs{\ee^{-st}}=\ee^{-t\Re s}∣e−st∣=e−tRes, so the integral (26.2) converges absolutely exactly when fff is transformable at Re⁡s\Re sRes; the imaginary part Im⁡s\Im sIms does not matter.

26.2 Analyticity in the half-plane

As for Lecture 24’s strip theorem, the proof applies Lecture 18’s lemma on analytic parameter integrals, here to the entire functions s↦e−stf(t)s\mapsto\ee^{-st}f(t)s↦e−stf(t). As in Lectures 22–25, each use of the standing rules I1–I3 of Lecture 22 (dominated limits, differentiation under the integral sign, Fubini–Tonelli) names the rule.

The last part of Theorem 26.4 is a test. A function that does not tend to 000 as Re⁡s→∞\Re s\to\inftyRes→∞, such as a nonzero constant, s/(s+1)s/(s+1)s/(s+1) or es\ee^{s}es, is not the transform of any transformable function. Section 26.3 shows that the constant 111 is the transform of an impulse.

Reading a table of transforms from right to left, to recover fff from FFF, needs a uniqueness theorem, which Lecture 27 proves. Until then this lecture computes transforms only forward. When it identifies a signal from its transform, it checks the signal by an independent argument.

26.3 Data at the initial instant and impulses

A switch closed at t=0t=0t=0, or a hammer blow at t=0t=0t=0, separates the state of a system just before the instant, at t=0−t=0^-t=0−, from the state just after it, at t=0+t=0^+t=0+, which the impulse has changed. For a function yyy on R\RR with one-sided limits at 000 we write y(0−)y(0^-)y(0−) and y(0+)y(0^+)y(0+) for these limits, as in Lecture 22, and [y]0=y(0+)−y(0−)[y]_0=y(0^+)-y(0^-)[y]0​=y(0+)−y(0−) for the jump.

Lecture 22 left open what the integral of an impulse at an endpoint of the interval of integration means. The expression ∫0∞δ(t)g(t) ⁣dt\int_0^\infty\dirac(t)g(t)\dd t∫0∞​δ(t)g(t)dt is not a pairing with a test function, and the rectangle families on [0,ε][0,\varepsilon][0,ε], on [−ε,0][-\varepsilon,0][−ε,0] and on [−ε/2,ε/2][-\varepsilon/2,\varepsilon/2][−ε/2,ε/2] give the limits g(0)g(0)g(0), 000 and g(0)/2g(0)/2g(0)/2. For the Laplace transform we fix the first choice. An impulse at the instant a≥0a\ge0a≥0 is the limit of short forces that act just after aaa, so it belongs to the motion for t≥at\ge at≥a. Indeed, let the profile η\etaη be piecewise continuous, vanish outside [0,1][0,1][0,1] and have ∫η ⁣du=1\int\eta\dd u=1∫ηdu=1. Since ηε(t−a)\eta_\varepsilon(t-a)ηε​(t−a) vanishes for t<at<at<a, and e−st\ee^{-st}e−st is continuous on R\RR, Lecture 22’s lemma on nascent deltas, in its form for a profile that vanishes outside a bounded interval, gives ∫0∞e−stηε(t−a) ⁣dt=∫−∞∞e−stηε(t−a) ⁣dt⟶e−sa(ε→0+),\int_0^\infty\ee^{-st}\eta_\varepsilon(t-a)\dd t=\int_{-\infty}^\infty\ee^{-st}\eta_\varepsilon(t-a)\dd t \longrightarrow\ee^{-sa}\qquad(\varepsilon\to0^+),∫0∞​e−stηε​(t−a)dt=∫−∞∞​e−stηε​(t−a)dt⟶e−sa(ε→0+), also for a=0a=0a=0. The following definition records this choice.

Definition 26.6 (Signals with impulses and the 0−0^-0− convention). A signal with impulses is a formal sum y=g+∑jpj δ(t−tj),y=g+\sum_jp_j\,\dirac(t-t_j),y=g+j∑​pj​δ(t−tj​), where ggg is transformable, the distinct impulse times tj≥0t_j\ge0tj​≥0 have finitely many members in each bounded interval, the weights pjp_jpj​ are complex numbers, and ∑j∣pj∣e−ctj<∞\sum_j\abs{p_j}\ee^{-ct_j}<\infty∑j​∣pj​∣e−ctj​<∞ for a real ccc at which ggg is transformable. Its Laplace transform is L ⁣[y](s)=G(s)+∑jpje−stj(Re⁡s≥c),\LT{y}(s)=G(s)+\sum_jp_j\ee^{-st_j}\qquad(\Re s\ge c),L[y](s)=G(s)+j∑​pj​e−stj​(Res≥c),(26.10) where an impulse at tj=0t_j=0tj​=0 counts in full. This is the 0−0^-0− convention: the transform integral is read as an integral over [0−,∞)[0^-,\infty)[0−,∞).

The series in (26.10) converges absolutely for Re⁡s≥c\Re s\ge cRes≥c, because ∣e−stj∣≤e−ctj\abs{\ee^{-st_j}}\le\ee^{-ct_j}∣e−stj​∣≤e−ctj​. Two signals with impulses are equal when their regular parts agree except at finitely many points in each bounded interval and their impulses have the same times and weights; an equation between such sums is read in this way. A single impulse gives L ⁣[δ](s)=1,L ⁣[δ(t−a)](s)=e−as(a≥0, s∈C).\LT{\dirac}(s)=1,\qquad\LT{\dirac(t-a)}(s)=\ee^{-as}\qquad(a\ge0,\ s\in\C).L[δ](s)=1,L[δ(t−a)](s)=e−as(a≥0, s∈C).(26.11)

L ⁣[δ](s)=1,L ⁣[δ(t−a)](s)=e−as(a≥0, s∈C).\LT{\dirac}(s)=1,\qquad\LT{\dirac(t-a)}(s)=\ee^{-as}\qquad(a\ge0,\ s\in\C).L[δ](s)=1,L[δ(t−a)](s)=e−as(a≥0, s∈C).(26.11)

The derivative of a function with jumps contains impulses, by the jump formula of Lecture 22. A function yyy on R\RR is piecewise C1C^1C1 in the sense of Lecture 23: every bounded interval has a finite partition such that on each open piece yyy is differentiable and yyy and y′y'y′ extend continuously to the closed piece. We write y′y'y′ for the ordinary derivative, defined off the exceptional points.

Theorem 26.7 (Derivative rule). Let yyy be piecewise C1C^1C1 on R\RR, let tjt_jtj​ be its exceptional points in (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞), with the jumps [y]tj=y(tj+)−y(tj−)[y]_{t_j}=y(t_j^+)-y(t_j^-)[y]tj​​=y(tj+​)−y(tj−​). Put Dy=y′+[y]0 δ(t)+∑tj>0[y]tj δ(t−tj),Dy=y'+[y]_0\,\dirac(t)+\sum_{t_j>0}[y]_{t_j}\,\dirac(t-t_j),Dy=y′+[y]0​δ(t)+tj​>0∑​[y]tj​​δ(t−tj​),(26.12) the terms of Lecture 22’s jump formula at the times t≥0t\ge0t≥0. Then for Re⁡s≥c\Re s\ge cRes≥c L ⁣[y′](s)=sY(s)−y(0+)−∑tj>0[y]tje−stj(0+ form),\LT{y'}(s)=sY(s)-y(0^+)-\sum_{t_j>0}[y]_{t_j}\ee^{-st_j}\qquad(0^+\text{ form}),L[y′](s)=sY(s)−y(0+)−tj​>0∑​[y]tj​​e−stj​(0+ form),(26.13)L ⁣[Dy](s)=sY(s)−y(0−)(0− form).\LT{Dy}(s)=sY(s)-y(0^-)\qquad(0^-\text{ form}).L[Dy](s)=sY(s)−y(0−)(0− form).(26.14) If yyy is continuous at every point t≥0t\ge0t≥0 of R\RR, then y(0−)=y(0+)=y(0)y(0^-)=y(0^+)=y(0)y(0−)=y(0+)=y(0), Dy=y′Dy=y'Dy=y′ for t≥0t\ge0t≥0, and both forms reduce to L ⁣[y′](s)=sY(s)−y(0)\LT{y'}(s)=sY(s)-y(0)L[y′](s)=sY(s)−y(0).

Mechanical problems have a continuous position and a velocity that may jump. Applying the theorem twice gives the rule for a second derivative.

Proposition 26.8 (Second derivative). Let yyy be continuous and piecewise C1C^1C1 on R\RR, and let vvv be piecewise C1C^1C1 on R\RR and equal to y′y'y′ off the exceptional points of yyy. Proof. Theorem 26.7 for vvv gives L ⁣[Dv]=sL ⁣[v]−v(0−)\LT{Dv}=s\LT v-v(0^-)L[Dv]=sL[v]−v(0−). Since yyy is continuous, the same theorem for yyy gives L ⁣[v]=L ⁣[y′]=sY−y(0)\LT v=\LT{y'}=sY-y(0)L[v]=L[y′]=sY−y(0). Substituting the second formula into the first gives (26.16). ■

Here DvDvDv is the second distributional derivative of yyy at the times t≥0t\ge0t≥0, as in Lecture 22’s struck oscillator, and v(0−)=y′(0−)v(0^-)=y'(0^-)v(0−)=y′(0−) is the velocity before the initial instant.

Example 26.9 (An impulse at the initial instant). We transform an equation whose input contains an impulse at t=0t=0t=0 in three ways, two of which are correct. We use Lecture 25’s RC filter try′+y=ft_{\mathrm r}y'+y=ftr​y′+y=f, where yyy is the capacitor voltage and tr>0t_{\mathrm r}>0tr​>0 the time constant. Before t=0t=0t=0 the voltage approaches y(0−)=y0y(0^-)=y_0y(0−)=y0​. At t=0t=0t=0 the input delivers the impulse f=p δ(t)f=p\,\dirac(t)f=pδ(t) of weight ppp, and for t>0t>0t>0 the input is zero.

The equation holds as trDy+y=p δ(t)t_{\mathrm r}Dy+y=p\,\dirac(t)tr​Dy+y=pδ(t) for t≥0t\ge0t≥0. Comparing the impulses at t=0t=0t=0 on the two sides gives tr[y]0=pt_{\mathrm r}[y]_0=ptr​[y]0​=p, so y(0+)=y0+p/try(0^+)=y_0+p/t_{\mathrm r}y(0+)=y0​+p/tr​. For t>0t>0t>0 the voltage solves try′+y=0t_{\mathrm r}y'+y=0tr​y′+y=0 with this initial value, so y(t)=(y0+p/tr)e−t/try(t)=(y_0+p/t_{\mathrm r})\ee^{-t/t_{\mathrm r}}y(t)=(y0​+p/tr​)e−t/tr​ by Lecture 5. Its transform, by (26.4) with σ=−1/tr\sigma=-1/t_{\mathrm r}σ=−1/tr​, is Y(s)=y0+p/trs+1/tr=try0+p1+str(Re⁡s>−1tr).Y(s)=\frac{y_0+p/t_{\mathrm r}}{s+1/t_{\mathrm r}}=\frac{t_{\mathrm r}y_0+p}{1+st_{\mathrm r}}\qquad\Bigl(\Re s>-\frac1{t_{\mathrm r}}\Bigr).Y(s)=s+1/tr​y0​+p/tr​​=1+str​tr​y0​+p​(Res>−tr​1​).(26.17) We now compare three bookkeepings.

  • The 0−0^-0− form with the impulse kept. The rule (26.14) and L ⁣[δ]=1\LT{\dirac}=1L[δ]=1 give tr(sY−y0)+Y=pt_{\mathrm r}(sY-y_0)+Y=ptr​(sY−y0​)+Y=p, which is (26.17).

Either the data at 0−0^-0− with every impulse kept, or the data at 0+0^+0+ with the impulse at 000 removed, gives the motion. The two must not be combined. ◃

26.4 Operational rules

The first rule is linearity. If fff and ggg are transformable at ccc and z1,z2∈Cz_1,z_2\in\Cz1​,z2​∈C, then z1f+z2gz_1f+z_2gz1​f+z2​g is transformable at ccc by the triangle inequality and comparison (GM 27), and L ⁣[z1f+z2g](s)=z1F(s)+z2G(s)(Re⁡s≥c),\LT{z_1f+z_2g}(s)=z_1F(s)+z_2G(s)\qquad(\Re s\ge c),L[z1​f+z2​g](s)=z1​F(s)+z2​G(s)(Res≥c), by the linearity of the integral.

Proposition 26.10 (Shift, scaling and delay). Let fff be transformable at a real number ccc, and let F=L ⁣[f]F=\LT fF=L[f].

Proposition 26.18 (The matrix exponential and the resolvent). Let AAA be a constant n×nn\times nn×n matrix with the column-sum norm ∥A∥\norm A∥A∥ of Lecture 11. Summary

The Laplace transform of a signal on t>0t>0t>0 is analytic on a half-plane, a property of the signal and not of a formula; the operational rules turn delays, integrals, convolutions and impulses at 0−0^-0− into algebra on it.

  • Half-plane: cf=inf⁡{c:∫0∞e−ct∣f∣ ⁣dt<∞}c_f=\inf\{c:\int_0^\infty\ee^{-ct}\abs f\dd t<\infty\}cf​=inf{c:∫0∞​e−ct∣f∣dt<∞}; ∣f∣≤Mecet\abs f\le M\ee^{c_{\mathrm e}t}∣f∣≤Mece​t for t≥tet\ge t_{\mathrm e}t≥te​ and ∫0te∣f∣<∞\int_0^{t_{\mathrm e}}\abs f<\infty∫0te​​∣f∣<∞ give cf≤cec_f\le c_{\mathrm e}cf​≤ce​; L ⁣[eσt]=1/(s−σ)\LT{\ee^{\sigma t}}=1/(s-\sigma)L[eσt]=1/(s−σ) for Re⁡s>Re⁡σ\Re s>\Re\sigmaRes>Reσ only.

  • Analyticity: FFF is analytic for Re⁡s>cf\Re s>c_fRes>cf​, F(n)=L ⁣[(−t)nf]F^{(n)}=\LT{(-t)^nf}F(n)=L[(−t)nf], F(s)→0F(s)\to0F(s)→0 as Re⁡s→∞\Re s\to\inftyRes→∞; L ⁣[tν]=Γ(ν+1)/sν+1\LT{t^\nu}=\Gamma(\nu+1)/s^{\nu+1}L[tν]=Γ(ν+1)/sν+1 for ν>−1\nu>-1ν>−1, Re⁡s>0\Re s>0Res>0.
